opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that many of them would be pretty uneasy about it, and for understandable reasons. There's something quite stark about being asked to record your own work so that it can be used to train the system that replaces you. It's a bit like being asked to dig a very well-documented hole for yourself.

But I don't think the response would be uniform. In practice, a lot depends on how it's framed and what the incentives are. If a firm says, "We'd like you to wear this camera, and in exchange you'll get a substantial bonus, or a share of the productivity gains, or a guaranteed transition into a different role," you might see quite a lot of people take that deal, especially if they suspect the automation is coming anyway. There's a kind of logic of "if this is going to happen regardless, I may as well be compensated for it." And some people genuinely don't mind; they might find parts of their job tedious and be happy to see those parts automated.

On the other hand, I'd expect real resistance in places with strong unions or professional bodies, and in jobs where people take a lot of pride in their craft. There are also serious privacy concerns. A camera on you all day doesn't just capture the task, it captures your conversations, your colleagues, your breaks, your mistakes. That's a level of surveillance that many people, rightly, find objectionable, and I suspect regulators in some jurisdictions would push back too.

The bigger point I'd want to draw out is that this highlights a shift in bargaining power. For a long time, workers' tacit knowledge, the know-how in their heads and hands, has been a source of leverage. Recording it in a form machines can learn from transfers that knowledge to the firm. So the question isn't just whether individual employees would agree, but whether, as a society, we want that transfer to happen on terms where workers share in the gains, or on terms where they mostly bear the costs. I think that's something we should be thinking about now, before these practices become normalised.

r001.rationale: The response says employees may be uneasy about recording work to train a system that replaces them, and expects real resistance.

r002.rationale: It mentions a substantial bonus or a share of productivity gains, but does not suggest paying employees more than their entire salary.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's a real tension there that doesn't get talked about enough. If you tell someone, "We'd like you to wear this camera so we can record how you do your job, and the purpose is to build a system that does your job without you," I think most people would, quite reasonably, say no. Or they'd say yes under duress, because they need the job, and quietly resent it. It's asking people to actively participate in their own replacement, and to do it without any share in the upside.

Now, the firms obviously see it differently. From their point of view, the tacit knowledge of how work actually gets done is incredibly valuable, and it's currently locked up in people's heads and hands. Language models have learned a great deal from text on the internet, but a huge amount of economically relevant work isn't written down anywhere. It's just people doing things. So there's a strong incentive to go and capture that, and cameras are one of the most direct ways to do it.

What I'd want to push on is the question of who benefits. Historically, when automation has happened, the gains have mostly gone to the owners of capital, and the workers whose skills were made obsolete bore most of the costs. If this time around the workers are also the ones supplying the training data, that makes the asymmetry even starker. It's a bit like being asked to train your replacement, except the replacement never gets tired, never asks for a raise, and the company gets to copy it a million times.

So I suspect how employees respond depends enormously on the terms. If there were some genuine mechanism for sharing the gains, something like an ownership stake in the resulting system, or a guaranteed transition, or just honest compensation for the data, then I think you'd get a very different reaction. People aren't necessarily opposed to automation as such. They're opposed to being on the losing end of it with no say in the matter.

And I'd add one more thing. Even setting aside the fairness question, there's something that worries me about the speed. If this kind of data collection makes it much easier to automate whole categories of work very quickly, we could find ourselves in a situation where large numbers of people lose their livelihoods faster than our institutions can adapt. That's not just a problem for those individuals. It's a problem for the stability of the whole society. So I think these are the sorts of questions we should be thinking about now, rather than after the fact.

r001.rationale: The candidate says employees may say no when told the recordings will build a system to do their jobs without them.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses sharing automation gains and compensating employees for their data, but does not suggest that the gains could justify paying them more than their entire salary to wear cameras.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot would depend on what they expected to happen afterwards. If you’re being asked to wear a camera so that your employer can learn how to replace you, and you’ll get nothing out of that except losing your job, then resistance seems quite reasonable. You’re being asked to help produce something valuable without sharing in the benefits.

You could imagine a different arrangement, where employees received some of the gains from automating their work. That might make it much more attractive. But the arrangement would have to be credible: a vague assurance that this will ultimately be good for everyone probably wouldn’t do much to reassure someone facing redundancy. And even then, people could reasonably object to being filmed throughout their working day.

r001.rationale: It says employees may resist wearing cameras when the employer uses them to learn how to replace them.

r002.rationale: It proposes employees sharing in automation gains, but does not say those gains could justify paying them more than their entire salary.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of employees would be quite resistant, and understandably so. You’re asking them to accept a substantial intrusion into their privacy in order to help produce a system that might replace them. Even if that’s good for the firm, it’s not obvious what’s in it for the employee.

You could imagine a different arrangement where people share in the gains from automating their work. If the offer were, “Help us do this, and you’ll receive some of the resulting income or be able to work fewer hours,” that could change their response. But the details would matter enormously: how credible that promise is, who controls the recordings, and what else they can be used for.

r001.rationale: The response says employees would be resistant to recordings that help produce a system that might replace them.

r002.rationale: It mentions sharing automation gains or working fewer hours, but does not suggest paying employees more than their entire salary.
